sections.title: Taxonomy and general form
sections.text: Penicillium roqueforti Thom is a microscopic filamentous fungus in the phylum Ascomycota (Eurotiales, Aspergillaceae). It does not form a cap-and-stem fruiting body. In laboratory culture, colonies may be velvety or more fasciculate, often blue-green to grey-green, but colour and texture vary with strain and growth medium.

sections.title: Microscopic morphology
sections.text: The mycelium consists of septate hyphae. Erect conidiophores, with rough-walled stipes, usually end in brush-like branching at several levels (often terverticillate, though other architectures also occur). Phialides produce loose chains of asexual conidia that are spherical, smooth and dark green, about 3–4.5 µm in diameter. An isolate cannot be identified from colour alone; microscopy and appropriate taxonomic methods are among the evidence used.

sections.title: Ecology and food role
sections.text: This mould is best known as a ripening culture that contributes to the blue veins and flavour of blue-veined cheeses such as Roquefort, Gorgonzola and Stilton. It also occurs outside dairies, including in soil, wood, silage and foods where it can cause spoilage. Populations and morphology differ among strains and environments.

sections.title: Metabolites and caution
sections.text: Some P. roqueforti strains can produce different secondary metabolites; some, including roquefortine C and PR toxin, are studied for their toxicological effects. Production depends on strain and conditions. This does not mean every blue cheese contains a hazardous amount, nor that any unknown blue mould is a food strain. This profile is not an assessment of food safety.

traits: Microscopic filamentous ascomycete mould; no cap-and-stem fruiting body
Culture colonies often blue-green to grey-green, velvety to fasciculate; appearance varies with strain and medium
Septate hyphae; erect conidiophores with rough-walled stipes ending in branched brush-like heads
Phialides producing chains of spherical, smooth, dark-green asexual conidia (about 3–4.5 µm)
Ripening culture for blue-veined cheeses, but also a spoilage mould in various foods and silage
safetyNote: Selected strains are used in controlled food production. The ability to produce some metabolites varies by strain and conditions; blue-green appearance alone cannot identify P. roqueforti or establish that food is safe. Do not eat mouldy food based on this profile.
